title: Chapter 27: Reading and Improving Code with AI
video_title: Python Chapter 27: Reading and Improving Code with AI
summary: Asha finds Sam's old till code at the Corner Cafe: short names, magic numbers and no tests. Follow her as she reads it, records what it does with tests and refactors it in small steps. Then watch her tidy a stock checker with an AI assistant at all six stages, where runs and tests catch three AI mistakes.

scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Define refactoring, and why tests come first.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: Most programming work is changing code that already exists.
**Refactoring** means changing the structure of code without changing what it does.
Tests, written before any change, prove the behaviour stayed the same.

segments.say: Most programming work is changing code that already exists, often written by someone else.
Refactoring means changing the structure of code, without changing what it does. And the proof is a set of tests, written before you change anything.

scenes.title: The idea: a safe refactoring loop
scenes.direction: Teach the loop, characterization tests and the diff format, then a breather. The kitchen analogy stays in the lesson.

visual.heading: A safe refactoring loop
visual.label: The idea
body: Go round the loop once for **every** small change.
visual.pre:
1. Tests first        record what the code does now
          |
  2. One small change   rename, a constant, a new function
          |
  3. Run the tests      same results?  yes: keep it
          |                            no:  undo it
  4. Review             read the change, then repeat

segments.say: Here is the big idea: a safe refactoring loop. First, tests that record what the code does now.
Then one small change. Then run the tests. Same results? Keep it. Different? Undo it. Then review, and go round again.
A test that records what the code does now, even the odd parts, is called a characterization test. It does not ask whether the result is right. It asks whether it is the same as before.

visual.heading: How to read a diff
visual.label: The idea
body: A **diff** shows two versions of a file, line by line.
visual.pre:
--- old version
  +++ new version
  @@ where a group of changes starts @@
   a line that did not change
  -a line that was removed
  +a line that was added

segments.say: To review a change, you read a diff. A diff shows two versions of a file, line by line.
A line that starts with minus was removed. A line that starts with plus was added. A line that starts with a space did not change.

items: Refactoring keeps the behaviour.
Tests first, then one small change.
In a diff, minus was removed and plus was added.

segments.say: Breather. Tests first, then one small change at a time.
Next, Asha reads Sam's code.

scenes.title: Step 1: Read from the top
scenes.direction: Read till_old part by part, then ask about the empty order. Then trace one input with prints, and ask about the second pass.

visual.heading: Step 1: Read from the top

segments.say: Step 1. Before you change anything, read the code from the first line, and say in words what each part does. Line 2 defines f, with two values, a and b.
Lines 4 and 5 go through a. Each x is a tuple, so x 1 and x 2 are its second and third values. So a is an order of name, price and count.
Line 6 checks b, and line 7 takes 10 percent off. So b says whether the customer is a member.
Line 8 adds tax, and line 9 rounds. Lines 14 to 16 call f three times.

ask.question: What does line 16 print, for an empty order?

after.say: Zero point zero. The loop never runs, so t stays 0. But 0 times 1.1 is a float, so round gives 0.0, not 0.
Lines 14 and 15 print 12.38, and 11.14 for a member. Remember these three results.

visual.heading: Step 1: Trace one input

segments.say: To check her reading, Asha traces one input. Line 8 prints the running total inside the loop, as in Chapter 9.
On the first pass, two teas at 3.5 make 7.0.

ask.question: What does line 8 print on the second pass?

after.say: Cake, 4.25, 1, t equals 11.25. 7.0, plus one cake.
And with tax, 12.38. Asha's reading of the code was right.

scenes.title: Step 2: Characterization tests
scenes.direction: Asha records the three results from Step 1 as pytest tests, run them, then a quiz on the idea.

visual.heading: Step 2: Record what it does now

segments.say: Step 2. Now Asha records what f does today, before any change. Line 2 imports f, and line 4 is the order from step 1.
Each test uses one result from step 1. The normal order, the member order, and the odd one: an empty order gives 0.0.
She runs pytest. Three dots, three passed. From now on, any change that breaks one of them has changed the behaviour.

visual.question: Why does Asha's test expect `0.0` for an empty order, even though it looks odd?
options: Because the test records what the code does now
visual.explain: A characterization test records the current behaviour, odd parts included.

segments.say: Quick check. Why does Asha's test expect 0.0 for an empty order?

after.say: C. A characterization test records what the code does now. It is not a judgement of right or wrong.

scenes.title: Step 3: Rename for the reader
scenes.direction: Rename f, a, b and t. Tests call the new name, with the same expected values. Ask what pytest reports.

visual.heading: Step 3: Clear names
visual.hidden_text: The tests run on the next screen.

segments.say: Step 3: the first small change, the names. F becomes order total, a becomes items, and b becomes is member.
Line 4 unpacks each tuple into name, price and count, as in Chapter 13. So x 1 and x 2 disappear.
And t 2 becomes with tax, a name that says what it holds.

visual.heading: Step 3: The tests, on the new name

segments.say: The tests change in one way only: line 2 imports the new name. Every expected value stays exactly as it was.

ask.question: Asha changed only names. What will pytest report?

after.say: Three passed. The names changed, and the behaviour did not.

scenes.title: Step 4: Name the magic numbers
scenes.direction: Teach magic numbers and constants, run the tests, then read the diff between Step 3 and Step 4. Quiz, breather.

visual.heading: Step 4: Constants for magic numbers
visual.hidden_text: The tests run on the next screen.

segments.say: Step 4. A magic number is a number in the code with no name, like 0.1 or 1.1. A reader cannot tell what it means.

A constant gives it a name. By convention, constants are written in capital letters, at the top of the file. Python will not stop a change, but the capitals tell people not to. Lines 11 and 12 now use the names.
Then she runs the tests.

visual.heading: Step 4: The tests, again

segments.say: Line 2 imports the version with constants. Three passed, again.

visual.heading: Step 4: Read the change as a diff

segments.say: Now Asha reviews the change. The diff lib module compares till v 2, from step 3, with till v 3, from step 4. Lines 7 and 8 skip the file comment on line 1 of each file.
On line 9, v 2 and v 3 are the labels for the two versions, and n equals 1 shows one unchanged line around each change.
The plus lines at the top add the two constants.
And these minus and plus pairs swap 0.1 and 1.1 for their names. Every other line is unchanged.

visual.question: In a unified diff, what does a line that starts with `-` mean?
visual.explain: Minus lines were removed, plus lines were added, and a space means no change.

segments.say: Quick check. In a diff, what does a line that starts with minus mean?

after.say: B. It was removed. Plus means added.

items: Read first, then trace one input.

segments.say: Breather. Two small changes done, and the tests passed after each one.
Next, the last step, and Sam's code side by side with Asha's.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the readable till
scenes.direction: Step 5 extracts subtotal. Walk the final module, show the tests, then run old and new side by side with an ask.

visual.heading: Step 5: Extract a function
visual.hidden_text: The tests run on the next screen.

segments.say: Step 5 extracts a function. The loop that adds up the order becomes its own function, subtotal, on lines 7 to 12, with a docstring.
Line 12 returns the total. Without that return, the result would never come back out.
Order total now calls subtotal on line 17, and takes off the discount. The name with tax is no longer needed, so the tax moves into the return, on line 20.
And line 2 is a docstring for the whole module.

visual.heading: Step 5: The tests, on the final version

segments.say: The tests pass on the final version too: three passed.

visual.heading: Mission check: old and new, side by side

segments.say: To be sure, Asha runs Sam's f, and her order total, side by side. Line 5 has three orders: the one from step 1, three juices, and an empty one.
Lines 6 and 7 try each order with and without the member discount. Line 10 prints the old result, the new result, and whether they are equal.

ask.question: What is the last word on every line that line 10 prints?

after.say: True, six times. Every pair is equal.
Mission complete! The code is easy to read, and it does exactly what Sam's code did.
But Sam left one more function, a stock checker. Asha decides to tidy it with an AI assistant, one stage at a time.

scenes.title: Work with AI: Sam's stock checker
scenes.direction: Safety first. Then the six stages on the stock checker. The explanation, the comparison, the rename and the sorted feature are each caught by a run or a test.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: a safe refactoring loop
visual.label: Before you start
items: Tests first, then the AI's suggestion, then your review, then the tests again.
Check every claim the AI makes with a real run.
Never paste private data. Use made-up stock numbers.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill: a safe refactoring loop. Tests first, then the AI's suggestion, then your review, then the tests again.
Check every claim with a real run. And never paste private data. Use made-up stock numbers.

visual.heading: Plan: ask for an explanation, not a change

messages.text: Someone else wrote this function. Do not change it. Explain what it does, in plain words.
chk takes the stock s and an order o. It returns the items that will run out after the order.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Sam's stock checker has the shortest names yet. Asha asks the AI to explain it, without changing it.
The AI says c h k returns the items that will run out after the order. It sounds sure.

visual.heading: Plan: check the claim with a run

segments.say: Asha checks the claim with a run. Line 6 calls c h k, and lines 7 and 8 print what is left of each item.
Cake has 2 left. It has not run out, but it is in the list. And Scone, with exactly 3 left, is not.
So c h k returns the items that will have fewer than 3 left. The AI's explanation was close, but wrong.

visual.heading: Write: Asha's own tests, from real runs
visual.label: Stage 2

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes her own characterization tests first, with the results of real runs.
Exactly 3 left is the boundary, so it gets its own test.
And one test checks that the results keep the order of the order: Scone, then Cake.

visual.heading: Write: her five tests, on Sam's code

segments.say: Here are her five tests. Line 12 expects an empty list for exactly 3 left. Line 21 expects Scone before Cake.
On Sam's code, all five pass.

visual.heading: Write: her tests first, then ask what is missing

messages.text: I wrote my own tests first, from real runs. Which inputs do they not cover yet?
You cover plenty left, exactly 3 left, 2 left, the order of the results and an empty order. You could add an item that is not in the stock.

segments.say: Then she asks the AI which inputs her tests do not cover yet.
It suggests an item that is not in the stock. A fair idea, for later.

visual.heading: Generate: one refactoring, same behaviour

messages.text: Refactor chk with clear names. Keep the behaviour exactly the same. Do not add features.
Here it is. The behaviour is exactly the same.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks for clear names, exactly the same behaviour, and no new features.
The AI gives her low stock, with a constant, and says the behaviour is exactly the same.

visual.heading: Generate: review the change as a diff

segments.say: Asha reads the change as a diff, this time with n equals 0, so no unchanged lines. Every name changed, c h k, s, o, r and k, so every line shows as changed: six minus lines, and nine plus lines.
So she reads them in pairs. Look at the old if line, and the new one.

ask.question: Every line changed. Which change can change the result?

after.say: The comparison. The old line says less than 3. The new line says less than or equal to LOW LIMIT. With less than or equal, exactly 3 left now counts as low.

visual.heading: Test: her tests on the AI's version

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Line 2 imports the AI's function with as c h k, like import math as m in Chapter 18. So the same five tests run on the new code.
One failed: the test for exactly 3 left. The AI changed the behaviour, and it said it had not.

visual.heading: Test: which line changed the behaviour?

messages.text: I ran my five tests on your version. One failed, and the old version passed it. Which line changed the behaviour?

Line 8. I changed < 3 to <= LOW_LIMIT, so an item with exactly 3 left now counts as low.
Fix: change <= back to <.

segments.say: She shows the AI the failing test, and asks which line changed the behaviour.
Now the AI names line 8, and the comparison. Change it back to less than.

visual.heading: Test: less than, put back
visual.hidden_text: The tests run on the next screen.

segments.say: Asha changes less than or equal back to less than, on line 8, and keeps the clear names.

visual.heading: Test: every test again

segments.say: Then she runs every test again. Five passed. A regression is a change that breaks something that used to work, and this rerun checks for one.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: After the rename, my report stopped working. First explain the cause. Then show the smallest fix.

Line 2 imports chk, but stock_v2 now only has low_stock.
Smallest fix: keep the old name as a second name, chk = low_stock, at the end of the module.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Then Asha's daily report stops working. She pastes the code and the full error, and asks for the cause first.
Cannot import name c h k. Her report still uses the old name. The AI suggests keeping the old name as a second name for the same function.

visual.heading: Debug: the old name, kept
visual.hidden_text: The report runs on the next screen.

segments.say: A function is a value, like a number, so line 14 can give it a second name, as the as keyword did on import. Now c h k and low stock lead to the same function.
And line 6 is a docstring with the true behaviour: fewer than 3 left.

visual.heading: Debug: the report, and every test again

segments.say: Her report imports c h k again, and it runs.

visual.heading: Debug: all five tests, on the final version

segments.say: And all five tests still pass on the final version. No regression.

visual.heading: Improve: one change, then every test

messages.text: My function passes all my tests. Suggest one improvement for readability only. It must not change any result.
Use a comprehension, and return sorted(low), so the list is tidier.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one readability change that keeps every result.
The AI suggests a comprehension, and sorted, so the list is tidier.

ask.question: Will all five of Asha's tests pass on this version?

after.say: No. Sorted puts Cake before Scone, so the test for the order fails. Sorting is a new feature that nobody asked for.

visual.heading: Improve: the order test catches it

segments.say: One failed: keeps order of the order.
A refactoring that changes the output is not a refactoring.

visual.heading: Improve: keep the comprehension, drop sorted
visual.hidden_text: The tests run on the next screen.

segments.say: So Asha keeps the part that helps, the comprehension on lines 7 and 8, and drops sorted. Line 9 returns the list as it is.

visual.heading: Improve: every test again

segments.say: She runs every test again. Five passed. That is a real improvement: clearer code, and the same behaviour.

visual.question: An AI says its refactoring keeps the behaviour exactly the same. What decides?
options: Your tests and a real run
How short the new code is
visual.explain: Only your tests and a real run show whether the behaviour stayed the same.

segments.say: Quick check. An AI says its refactoring keeps the behaviour. What decides?

after.say: A. Your tests, and a real run. Today they caught a wrong explanation, a changed comparison and a feature nobody asked for.

items: Check every AI claim with a run.
Read every AI change as a diff.
Run every test after every change.

segments.say: Breather. You watched Asha catch three AI mistakes, each with a run or a test.
Next, four mistakes people make when they refactor.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 shows too few test cases. Mistakes 2 and 3 are spot-it asks. Mistake 4 is changing a test to match.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: tests that cover too few cases

segments.say: Mistake 1. This tidy version rounds each line inside the loop, on line 8. It passes all three tests from step 2.
With two teas, both results are 11.14.
But with one tea, they are 7.67 and 7.68. Test several different inputs. And never move rounding into a loop during a refactoring.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 2. The function has a new name on line 2. Look at line 9.

after.say: It stops with a name error. F is not defined, because Python only knows the new name.
after.heading: Mistake 2: renaming, but not every call

after.say: The fix: change every call, or keep the old name as a second name, as Asha did with c h k.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 3. Lines 2 to 5 are an extracted function, subtotal. Line 9 uses its result.

after.say: A return. Without it, subtotal gives back None, and line 9 cannot multiply None by 1.1.
after.heading: Mistake 3: an extracted function with no return

after.say: The fix: return total, as on line 12 of the finished till.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: changing a test to match

segments.say: Mistake 4. This version forgot the member discount. Old says 11.14, new says 12.38.
Changing the test to expect 12.38 would hide the bug. Never change expected values during a refactoring. Undo the change instead.

items: Test several different inputs.
Rename every call, or keep the old name.
Never change a test to match new output.

segments.say: Breather. Now you know the four most common refactoring mistakes.
Two questions to think about on your own come next.

visual.question: During a refactoring, one of your tests fails. What do you do?
